sections.h: THIRD PART ZOSIME M. I. THE DIVINE ZOSIME ON VIRTUE (1). LESSON I
p: 1 . The composition of the waters, the movement, the increase, the removal and restitution of the corporeal nature, the separation of the spirit from the body, and the fixation of the spirit on the body; the operations which do not result from the addition of foreign and outward natures, but which are due to the proper, unique nature, acting on itself, derived from a single species, as well as (the use) of the liquids. This whole uniform and polychrome system includes the multiple and infinitely varied search for all things, the search for nature, subordinated to the lunar influence and the measurement of time, which regulate the term and growth according to which nature is transformed. When I said these things, I fell asleep; and I saw a priest standing before me, on top of an altar in the shape of a cup. This
AK (i)
"On the Virtue and Composition of Waters.
(2J) Separation of metals from volatile bodies, such as sulphur or arsenic, with which they are associated.

of flask (see the distillatory apparatus in fig. i i, 14. etc. , Introd. , p. 3. i32, i38 et seq. ; or rather kerotakisdesfig devices. 20,21 et seq. , Introd. , p. 3. 143 et seq.) All this is the mystical description of various chemical operations of distillationsublimation, cupellation, accompanied by roasting, effervescence, and color changes. 15-2

The altar had fifteen steps to climb. The priest stood there, and I heard a voice from on high saying to me: “I have done the work of going down the fifteen steps, walking towards the darkness, and the work of going up the steps, going towards the light. It is the priest who renews me, rejecting the thick nature of the body. Thus consecrated priest by necessity, I become a spirit. Having heard the voice of him who stood on the altar in the form of a cup, I asked him who he was. And he answered me in a faint voice, saying, “I am Ion (i), the priest of the sanctuaries, and I suffer intolerable violence. Someone came in the morning hastily, and he raped me, smashing me with a sword, and dismembering me, according to the rules of combination. He removed all the skin from my head, with the sword he held (in his hand); he mixed the bones with the flesh (2) and made them burn with the fire of the treatment. This is how I learned, through the transformation of the body, to become spirit. This is the intolerable violence (which I have suffered).” As he was still talking to me, and I forced him to speak to me, his eyes became like blood, and he vomited all his flesh. p: This is the divine and great mystery; the object Fqn seeks. This is the All. From Him comes the All, and through Him is the All. Two natures, one essence; for one attracts the one; and one dominates the one. This is Silver Skin (2), Hermaphrodite, which always leaks (3), which is attracted to its own elements. It is the divine water, which everyone has ignored, whose nature is difficult to contemplate; for it is neither a metal, nor water always in motion, nor a (metallic) body; it is not dominated. It is ALL in all things; it has life and spirit and it is destructive. Whoever understands this has gold and silver. The power has been hidden, but it is deposited in Erotyl (4).

sections.h: AND ON THE FOUR METAL BODIES, ACCORDING TO DEMOCRITUS
p: The four bodies (metallic) serve as a support (i), and none of them volatilizes. That is why he did not speak of grilling (by insufflation) the composition; for if it were useful, he would have mentioned it expressly. He said, “Nothing has been left out, nothing has been postponed.” He also says, speaking of the golden liquor, "It stains any body," which applies to the four bodies. It is also for this reason that he quoted his master as saying: "Turning all substances"; thereby showing that it is not a question of blowing; but that the four (bodies) which serve as A (1) dyeing.

support are dyed and able to dye. He introduces Pammenes operating on sulfur (i) and saying that there is no need to roast; for the sulfur evaporates itself during cooking, since it itself dyed. Mary said, “Take away the sulphurous lead; wherever the sulphur enters, it dyes.” She wanted to show by this that we are not right to roast sulfur. She used names foreign to the arts in describing their operations. This is not the way those who operate do, when they talk about our copper or about some metal body. A sheet is made by means of two metals joined by fusion. The Philosopher takes this metal sheet and cuts it into pieces; if the alloy is melted, it is better. This is what they say: “It is not by means of a leaf... That way, if they talk about grilling, they’re not talking about an operation done outside, but hanging out their own work. For they roast the cooked matter, in order to take their own (principle) and tinctorial. They reject the cooked materials, and evaporate the unnecessary parts (2). They give other names to purified products. Thus they roast by insufflation, so as to isolate the clean and tinctorial principle. This is how we burn in cooking, we expel by insufflation all foreign materials, keeping the spirit useful and tinctorial. On the weights of raw and cooked (substances). From what the writings say in this regard, surely sulphur must be expelled by insufflation. This is what Mary wanted to make heard by saying: “You will find 5 parts less a quarter, that is to say less sulfur driven by insufflation. Similar to the end of her talk, she says that copper, in its iron curing, decreases by a third of its weight. She says that these changes are also accomplished when bleaching and yellowing; sulfurous caries (substances) dye, but vanish. We get rid of sulphurous substances by volatilization. The same is true of plants, when they are entirely dis(i) The word lead has been replaced by general speaking. i23, note 7. As it happens when they are cooked with Sulfur Skin, rejecting the woody part. It is not without reason that Agathode'mon says "and unified"; but in order that, penetrating into the depth of the metal of silver, the tinctorial matter may escape the destruction caused by fire. We therefore deprive ourselves of dyes derived from plants, knowing that metals cannot borrow the qualities of them, and thus receive the dye thoroughly. Qualities alone act; for the body cannot penetrate into the interior of the body. Aristotle said (i): “The qualities triumph over each other.” According to Agathodemon the metals placed at the top take volatile substances: this is how he borrows the spirit of chrysocolla. This word spirit obviously means a volatile substance and the sublimated vapors are of the same order. Such are: the white vapor, the vapor of the cinnabar, and
“a more black, wet, pure spirit” (2).

For every sublimated vapor is a spirit, and these are the tinctorial qualities. The divine Democritus thus speaks of whitening and Hermes of smoke. When they were useful, they admitted them in the treatments, but (by designating them) in riddles. That is why it is a mystery. He said, “I have written this in the chapter, ‘If you are wise.’ The steam of native sulfur, arsenic, and the white vapor of cinnabar. Agathodemon also says: "Arsenic is the soul of golden matter. After he has been rid of his thick and caustic part, and has abandoned his sulphurous body, then take the colouring part.” Steam is the spirit, the spirit that enters the body. The soul differs from the spirit. He calls the soul nature originally sulphurous and caustic (arsenic?) Under the purifying influence of fire one preserves the spirit, if one works according to the rules of art; for it cannot be destroyed. This is the useful thing, the tinctorial element. The operator needs a subtle intelligence, so that he recognizes the spirit that came out of the body and makes use of it, and

As he watches his departure, he attains the goal, that is, that the body be destroyed, (he takes care that) the spirit be destroyed at the same time. Now it was not destroyed, but it penetrated into the depth of the metal, when the operator did his work. Those who do not recognize when the work is timely, misinterpret it; for they see nothing but materials that have not taken back their bodies (metallic, burnt or incinerated materials). While they judge only the visible part of these things, the unfortunate, by a kind of punishment, let loose everything and they fail to avoid the reduction (of the product) to ashes (i). No other support for dyeing is mentioned in any passage of the writings, except copper alone. Thus Mary says that copper is treated and later burned. It is in this sense that it plays the role of support. Such is the role of copper or silver in our operation. We do not want to derive quality from it, and their bodies, by his death, become useless. Plants, too, are useless, for they are consumed by fire. Agathodemon says, "Magnesy, antimony, and litharge vanish, having lost their purity." Mary said, “Blow the vapors, until the sulfurous products are volatilized with the shadow (which obscures the metal), and the copper takes all its brilliance.” Thus our copper receives from them the sublimed vapor. Steam is the spirit of the body. The soul differs from the spirit.

sections.h: M. XIII. ON THE DIVERSITY OF COILED COPPER
p: Many prepare the burnt copper by means of sulfur (2). The treatises of the other authors say so with obscurity. Democritus alone expresses himself with generous clarity: "Throw on copper a quarter of sulphuric iron, that is, prepared by melting with magnetic stone, a quarter or half of sulphur; pour the product with lead from antimony and litharge. Then burn the composition obtained with pyrite, copper and iron, so that a suitable slag is formed. Throw in the sublimated vapor of arsenic (sulphur). The metal is bleached by sulfur vapor >' . Speaking of ceruse cooked with sulfur, he wants to speak of pure sulfur, as fit to change the molybdochalque into summer metal. When he says: "Whitened magnesia produces the same effect"; he means the cinnabar treated simultaneously. But someone will object: he spoke first of magnesi and pyrite. “The steam described above, you will cook in oil.” The steam described above is the whole formula; for it seems to include divine skin and oil. They say that it is necessary to operate with all liquids, wanting to make (by this) mean liquidity. Indeed, by all these words: vinegared brine, then oil, then honey and milk, we must understand the divine water. Saffron by itself is powerless to dye without the help of divine water; those who want to dye use it. Mary speaks of “the dissolution of the comaris and beyond celandine.” Democritus (place) in the last class of white liquids "lime water that flowed" through the filter, or through a sock.
All species are treated by maceration, using simple liquids; then the product is subjected to washing. This is how the bodies are washed.

After drying out, if the metal has become shiny, resume steaming, process substances that can yellow with divine water and gum, and fix (tincture! on a light fire (i). When you have made the fixation, remove the substance, and let drain on the residue of the preparation for 2, or 3, or 7, or 41 days. If you put money into it, you’ll have to pay for it too. Then let’s find the right time.

SHOULD WE UNDERTAKE THE WORK AT ANY TIME? 1 . It is necessary that we seek out what are the opportune moments. He said that the spirit, subject to the action of the sun, must be taken from the flowers, and macerated from the morning; then by every proper action of fire, gold becomes good for use. "For it is the work of the sun," said the great Hermes, "it is produced by it." Listen to Hermes saying that the softening of substances intended to be softened is done cold. He explained himself clearly on this point at the end of his writing on lead bleaching. He also talks about gold. “This is how the one who prepares the whole works.” This is also where he explained to himself what one should filter the whole by any filter. This has not escaped Agathodemon, and he is talking about washing the ore and its purification, (which takes place) when the unwashed and liquefied All goes through the filter or fits you. Hermes says: “She becomes like an innocent laundry (?) If a deposit is formed, it is proof that the substances and minerals are not sufficiently sprayed. Hermes explained himself strongly on these things when speaking of the screens. (1) It is a superficial j dyeing operation. Introduction, p. 3. 56, in gold, by varnish or by colouring  58 to 60.

“If the waters move in every direction, the screen itself seems to flow.” They must go down together, following the great Hermes, and then they immediately go up into the apparatus intended to carry out the cooking. We have set out these things in our speech, except in terms of timing. The opportune moment is that of summer, while the sun has a nature (favorable' for the operation. Mary takes care of this, describing the treatments of the small object (i): "The divine water will be lost for those who do not understand what has been written, namely that the product (useful) is returned upwards by the matras and the tube. But it is customary to designate by this water the vapor of sulphur and of arsenic sulphides. For this reason you have mocked me, because in one and the same speech I have exposed to you such a great mystery.” This divine water, bleached by bleaching matter, causes bleaching. If it is yellowed by yellowing materials, it causes yellowing. If it is blackened by means of couperose and gall nuts, it blackens and realizes the blackening of silver and that of our molybdochalque. I told you earlier about this molybdochalque, on the occasion of our traditional money. Thus the blackened water, attaching itself to our molybdochalque, gives it a fixed black dye; and although this dye is nothing, all initiates desire to know it. However, the water capable of taking on such a color produces a rough dye, the oil and honey being eliminated. The Philosopher also says that a small amount of native sulfur is enough to burn many species and that it softens stones and metals. In this water dissolves the sulfur composition, as he says when speaking of Androdamas. “If you put on apyre sulfur, you produce a golden liquor.” To make it act on the composition of substances, we postpone the composition of sulphurous materials. In the same way, it is boiled or cooked. "Understand," he said, "that if you put on apyrous sulphur, you produce a golden liquor. By means of a sawdust fire, on the kerotakis, distills the divine water, until it contains (the color) of gold. You will cook by waving slightly, and adding the motaria (3) of the sanda(i) Cp. Yellow raque. [And they said the motaria, because it is as thick as blood]. Cook the product strongly for 2 or 3 days, and after pressing, pour the residue of the preparation into each vase: and it is formed from the ios. Pebichius also said on this question: "Share the preparation in two parts, and put one half in a terracotta vase and the other half on copper;" wanting to make this understood in one (word): cooking, by (the vase) of terracotta, and Tiosis, by copper. Now he spoke previously of bleaching, saying that copper is burned in laurel wood; that is, native sulfur (along with copper) in the presence of laurel leaves (i). By this you can know the merit of the ancients, how clearly they have explained all things. Seeming to hide all things, they said clearly: "First, on light flames, so that the sulphur water is absorbed at the same time." As for these flames, Mary said: "the flames gradually" and then: "the fire; gradually"; in order to make it clear that it is necessary to operate according to a suitable progression, starting (from the moment) of the flame. The right time is the time of summer. Purple also requires a special time for dissolutions and coolings. Similarly, the tearing gum, to flow spontaneously, wants the proper nature of summer. However, I have heard from a few that our operation is carried out in all circumstances, and I hesitate to believe it (2).
In these words Democritus exposes these things to the Egyptian prophets: “I write to you, O Philaret, to expose to you all the power of God.”

Democritus named the four metallic bodies substances; by this he meant copper, iron, tin, and lead. Everyone uses them in both tinctures (gold and silver), and all substances undergo both tinctures. All substances have been recognized by the Egyptians as produced by lead alone; for it is from lead that the other three bodies come (i). He named substances fire-resistant materials, and materials that do not resist them: non-substances. Indeed, non-substances act in a proper manner, independently of fire. 11 said that they are generated by the action of appliances and combustion; while the true residue of the preparation, prepared without the action of fire, produces a stable tincture in white or yellow. The use of the fleeting preparation obtained by the flame destroys the yellowing of the defective molybdochalque, since it makes it disappear. On this point, we must not be mistaken. See how he expresses himself in this regard: ". Bring to a viscous consistency; coat with half of the preparation for cooking and tinctures with the rest, so that the color is fixed without the aid of fire. Non-substances are called sulphurous materials that are not fire-resistant. But the use of suitable liquids gives them the property of resisting fire and remaining stable there: for water combats the action of fire. That is why he says: Nature, acquiring in its own right the opposite quality, becomes solid and fixed, dominant and dominated. Thus it acquires the sulphurous quality proper, that which gives its name to the native sulphur water. Why is he also talking about the opposite? sections.h: M. XIX. THE FOUR BODIES ARE THE FOOD OF DYES
p: Mary says that copper is dyed first, and then it is dyed. Their bodies are the four bodies. Here are the dyes: (they include) the solid and liquid species of the catalog, as well as the plants; the solids, from the sublimated steam to the chrysocolla. As for all the liquid (species) in the catalog, in reality, it is divine water.

Thus, just as we are nourished by solids and liquids (united), and are coloured only by their own quality, even if they contain their copper, and even if we are not nourished by solids alone, or by isel liquids, so also is copper not. Indeed, when we have received only solid matter, we are inflamed, burned, poisoned; likewise also their copper. On the other hand, if we have taken only drinks, we are intoxicated, we have a heavy head, we have coloured toys, and we also vomit copper. When he has taken the color of gold, by the action of divine water, he is weighed down and rejected, and immediately afterwards (his hue) becomes fleeting. But when we have taken a good proportion of food composed of the two orders of matter, solid and liquid, we are fed reasonably; our cheeks are colored reasonably, and the nutritional faculty distributes the food in the stomach, because of its faculty of retaining it. In the same way also copper, receiving the solids on one side as food, feeds on the other side of the divine water united with the gum, as wine; it is colored, due to the lyo

of the power to retain that resides in him. Thus, in the above-mentioned book, she said: “The sulphurous are dominated and restrained by the sulphurous.” Hence the truth: “Nature charms, conquers, and dominates nature.” “So,” she says, “that man is composed of the four elements; so also copper; and as man results (from the association) of liquids, solids, and spirit; so also copper. Now Apollo, in his oracles, says that the spirit is steam: "And a spirit blacker, damper, purer" (i).
Mary spoke well of steam: “Copper does not dye, but is dyed; and when it has been dyed, then it dyes; when it has been nourished, it nourishes; when it has been completed, it completes.” Good health.

p: I have written, with regard to the four bodies which serve as supports, and to the extent which the raw and cooked composition entails about them (i.e. it is necessary to apply all this to the explanation of magnesia. It is necessary to say how one forms the (metallic) body of magnesia; and if the whitening varies according to the maceration, as I have told you previously. Leave it in front of the stove; let the stove be lit with wood and red cobathia bark, for the smoke of these barks makes everything white. If you gather the smoke, the magnesia absorbs it and it is bleached. Didn't we remind in the--the book, speaking of red cobathia, that we had to learn first of what magnesia the philosophers speak of? If it is simple (magnesia), coming from Cyprus, or compound magnesia, obtained by our art? Indeed, in delegating simple magnesia, they want to speak of the compound; but at the same time they meant the simple. It is in this way that art has been hidden by the double meaning attributed to the denominations. The philosopher Hermes, after the sea water, names the natron, the vinegar, the blood of the gnat, the juice of the styrax, the lame alum, and other similar substances, and he says: "Leave it before the furnace, as I have said before, with a fire of red cobathia barks, for the smoke of the red cobathia itself whitens everything, being white." Thus speaks Hermes; but we must know that the natron, the styrax, the shale alum, and the ash of palm branches are white sulfur, which whitens everything. p: They are vain and you undertake to make empty reasonings. Give up the society of people who have blinded minds and too inflamed imagination. It is necessary to pity these people, and to listen to the language of truth, from the mouths of men worthy to announce it. These people do not want help; they cannot bear to be taught by ravens, flattering themselves to be masters (themselves). They claim to be honored for their vain and empty (meaningful) reasoning. When it is desired to teach them what the degrees of truth are, they will not endure the knowledge of art, nor digest it. They want gold rather than reason. Heated by extreme insanity, they become incapable of reasoning and cannot wait for wealth. For if they were guided by reason, gold would accompany them and be in their power; for reason is the master of gold. Whoever clings to it, who desires it and unites with it, will find the gold placed before us, in the midst of the detours that keep it hidden. Reason is the indicator of all goods, as has been said somewhere (i). Philosophy is the knowledge of truth, and reveals the beings that exist. He who accepts reason will see the gold placed in front of his eyes. But those who cannot bear reason constantly walk in a vacuum, and undertake the most ridiculous acts. Thus the laughter was provoked by Nilus, this priest your friend, who cooked the molybdochalque in a country oven (as if he had cooked bread), operating with the cobathia for a whole day. Blinded by the eyes of the body, he did not think that his procedure was bad, but he breathed; and coming out (the product) after cooling, he showed only ash. When asked where the bleaching was, embarrassed, he said he had penetrated deep. Then he put on copper, dyed the slag; for the copper being stopped by no solid, passed over and disappeared itself in the depth; likewise for the whitening of magnesia. Having heard these things (from the mouth) of his opponents, Paphnutia was greatly mocked; and you will be, too, if you fall into the same madness. Kiss for me Nilus, the one who cooks

Thus, converting and transmuting (he, in these authors, means giving a body to incorporeals, that is to say to fleeting matter. By their transformation we obtain the molybdochalque, the black lead, the one that must be treated with mercury, and become the body of magnesia. They do not mean, as some do, that the mutation applies to converting and transmuting mercury. But when the fleeting materials have taken a body, the conversion takes place for all bodies, by their tincture in white or yellow. Indeed this conversion is called transmutation, after the incorporeals have taken a body, by the effect of art. In the retrograde conversion accomplished by fire, that is to say in bleaching or yellowing, the substances released strongly and associated by fire, are of new calf made fleeting and become again incorporeal (2). At this point they are reduced to the last degree of division. Sublimated steam, the first of incorporeal materials, thus leads to the supreme art. They had everywhere to obey destiny, for the things already said and for their opposites, without being able to imagine anything else, relative to corporeal beings; (I say) nothing but the fatal order of destiny. The men of this species, Hermes, in the treatise on Natures, called them fools, fit only to conduct a procession to destiny, but incapable of understanding anything incorporeal things, or even of conceiving the destiny that leads them with justice. Corn they insult his teachings on corporeal beings, and they indulge in imaginations foreign to their own happiness. Hermes and Zoroaster have declared that the race of philosophers is superior to destiny. Indeed, they do not enjoy the happiness that comes from it. Dominating her pleasures, they are not affected by the evils she causes; always living in their innermost being, they do not accept the beautiful gifts she offers, because they see the unfortunate end of it. For this reason Hesiod presents Prometheus giving advice to Epimetheus: “What is the happiness that men judge to be the greatest of all? A beautiful woman, they say, with a lot of money. He says that he receives no present from Olympian Jupiter; but he rejects them, teaching his brother that he must reject, in the name of philosophy, the gifts of Jupiter, that is, the gifts of destiny. As for Zoroaster, boasting of the knowledge of all higher things and of those of magic, he says that he turns away from the language of corporeal beings; that everything that comes from destiny is evil, either in detail or in the whole. Hermes, however, speaking of external things, condemns magic, saying that the spiritual man, the one who knows himself himself, does not succeed in anything by magic, and does not look as if he were a spiritual man.

The whole kingdom of Egypt (i), O Woman, depends on these two arts, that of suitable dyes and that of minerals. Art called divine, either in its dogmatic and philosophical parts, or in most matters of lesser import, has been entrusted to sesgardicns for their subsistence.

This is so not only for this art, but also for the four years called liberals and for the manual arts. Their creative power belongs to kings. If they allow it, this one Fexposes orally, or Tintcrète after the steles, who has received the knowledge of it as an inheritance from his ancestors.

But he who possessed the knowledge of these things did not manufacture it (for himself), for he would have been punished; just as craftsmen who know how to mint the royal coin have no right to mint it for themselves, under penalty of punishment. So also, under the Egyptian kings, the artisans of the art of cooking and those who possessed the knowledge of the procedures did not operate for themselves; but they operated for the kings of Egypt, and worked for the sake of their treasures. They had particular chiefs placed at their head, and great was the tyranny exercised in the art of cooking, not only in itself, but also in that which dries up the gold mines. For as far as the excavation was concerned, it was a rule among the Egyptians that a written authorization was required.
Some blame Democritus and the ancients... (The continuation as on page 98, until the end of the paragraph.)

As for the proper tinctures, no one among the Jews or among the Greeks has ever exposed them. In elïet, they placed them in the images, shaped with their own colors and intended to preserve them.

The operations done on the minerals differ much from the suitable dyes. They were very jealous. K of the diulguation of art itself; and did not leave the manipulator without punishment. Anyone who conducts a search without authorization can be rushed (and put to death) by the overseers of the markets of the city, in charge of the collection of royal taxes. Similarly, it was not permissible to secretly make the stoves, or to secretly make suitable dyes. So you will not find anyone among the ancients who reveals what is hidden, and who exposes something clear in this regard. I have met only Democritus alone, among the ancients, who has made it clear something in this regard, in the enumerations of his catalogues.

Indeed, here is how he begins, in the preamble of his composition on liberal arts: here observes his malice. 11 spoke at the beginning of the mercury and the body of magnesia. And the others (substances! are all of the appropriate dye class. He expresses himself thus: "Attic ochre, minium du Pont, native sulphur: we take a pound of it; Phrygian stone, yellow sori, dry cut, cinnabar, misycuit, raw misy. You'll make androdamas, sulfur, arsenic, sandarachus. In order not to enumerate all that is in the four catalogues, you will find all the substances proper to the (tinctures) and for you to perform what he makes heard above, he has enumerated the raw (substances) and the cooked (substances) which correspond to the two arts. He speaks preferably of tinctures among the proper things.

When he says: misy raw, misycuit, yellow sori, dry couperose and the like; he speaks of the (substances) which have undergone a certain treatment, attaching themselves to the liberal arts. I will explain to you, with all the prophets, the power of the fires, so that your work is perfect and in accordance with the traditions, so as not to fail. In summer, the Philosopher explained, in speaking of fires, how the unity of the species is transformed by excessive fire; for the excess of fires is contrary to the whole operation. For the things to which you are previously exercised, I transmit to you the following precepts: If the sulphurous materials are cooked in glass vases, it is necessary to use the fires used by painters with kerotakis. It is necessary that the glass vase is filled with a ceramic lute, the thickness of half a finger; so that the vase does not break under the influence of heat. 111. Lvi. ON THE VAPORS I. They are called sublimated vapors, because of the fact that the substances are raised from the bottom up, above the ashes, towards the upper part, as it is exposed in the treatment of water. Thus they are called sublimated vapors, because of the fact that they rise from the bottom to the top of the apparatus, and we have explained how the suction of these condensed vapors or drops is carried out.

The dross is removed from the pot, it is discarded and the souls that have been drawn from it are projected upon them (i). These souls drawn from the (metallic) bodies, they sublimated them again by means of the udder-shaped apparatus, saying that this was the iosis, accomplished by the long-lasting reactions. They combined with the other sublimated vapors what they called bodies what we call a metallic body by operating with sulfurs, sulfides (acting on) copper, or asem leaves (2), or gold. This is how they dyed with the auxiliary materials, without taking into account their second treatment. He pointed to the filtered water (acting) on the ashes, saying: "Arrange the apparatus and bring the ashes; the ash experiences the action of the water, acting in the apparatus. Agathodemon says, “The ash is everything; it is on it that the decoction or the cooking is carried out, or else what is called the delaying. Thus, by means of decomposition, extraction, iosis, moderate cooking, the ancients said that the Whole is perfected. It is impossible to treat otherwise the manufacture (3) of the composition. For this fact that decoction and extraction are a delay is known to the interpreters of science. Iosis, they called it decoction; decoction and extraction, retardation, intended to produce extreme attenuation. Moreover they spoke of fire, because it produces heat, combustion, and flame. The ancients treated of childishness and womanly work the search for mere connoisseurs. But mus are not obliged for this reason to perform iosis by means of fire, as one operates for dyed stones, or in the treatment of liquids for cold-manufactured purple. I say that experience will teach us the truth; it will lead us to accomplish the one and perfect work and to (get) the stable projection powder. After the manufacture of this ios, they transported the vapors and islands) reunited with the remaining slags, and in this way they came to an end.

They are called pyrites (or their signs), which are almost the same.

It was then that they projected the tinctorial powder on the bodies, whereas Zosimas said: “Thus the spirits take a body and the dead bodies are revived by Fôme which comes from them, and which is again received in them. They carry out the divine work, two elements dominating each other and being dominated by each other. In fact, by this he obtains the fleeting spirit of the pursuing body (i), and he instructs us to make the tincture resistant to fire, by means of fire. Such, I think, according to the Philosopher, is the water of lime, or sandarachus, the water of natron, the water of lees, the water made with the ash of the sulphurous, the water of the first distillation. It must be rectified as the soapmakers’ laundry (2), and collect the water that comes from it: but the soapmakers’ laundry is never reduced to steam, but it is rectified (3). How then, O philosophers, can Zosimas say that the meaning of the scriptures is not understood, unless the apparatus which carries out the extraction on copper is employed? and that the term of the art is not that, but consists in the apparatus and in the fixation which is accomplished therein? Others used only vials for both types of compositions (5). After raising the water, they gathered it together with ordinary lime, releasing it in a mortar; not according to a precise measure, but in such a way that the dry part exceeded the liquid by two, three or four fingers.

( I ) This article is called Pelage, one of the old alchemists ( Cp. Olympidore, p. 96 and 194I; but it contains more modern additions and glosses. The text is very obscure and it is difficult to guarantee its exact meaning. However, it seems to relate to the gilding and silvering of metals, such as copper and iron: these metals must be previously oxidized from the sulphide to the surface, then decapitated and made shiny; then the gold or silver rendered "mitigated" is extended to their surface; that is to say, brought to a great state of division (powder and shell of gold), or else the silver may be made of amine. All this must, therefore, have originally expressed the fact that a metal is gilded or silvered by means of divided gold or silver, or a composition containing these bodies: then the idea of the transmutation of the very bottom of the metal was added. (2) Cp. Synesius, p. 3. 67. (3) Applied to metals, i.e. the art of transmutation. (4) Quality orgold orsilver color.

The ancients tell the truth when they say, “Copper does not dye, but is dyed, and when it has been dyed, it dyes (i).” It is for this reason that all the writings explain in similar terms the work of copper, and show how it is dyed: and if it is dyed, then it dyes; but if it is not dyed, it cannot dye, as has already been said.
That is why it is recommended to make the copper free of shadow, so that it becomes shiny it can receive the dye.

By the shadow of copper is meant the black tint it produces in silver. Indeed, you know that copper subjected to treatment (2) and projected on silver blackens it inside and outside: this blackening produces in silver, the writings call it shadow. This is why copper (3: until it can no longer produce blackening, when it is projected on silver.

Thus copper, as well as natural gold, must be treated until it no longer produces the slightest blackening in silver. This is why Democritus, too, said in his book on silver: “Verify whether copper has become shadowless; for if copper has not become shadowless, do not attack copper (from your failure), but yourself. » 3. Copper is treated with divine water, when it has experienced decomposition, when it has been laundered, cooked, and washed. "The lava," he said, "until all his ios is expelled. Remember, in this regard, what the philosophers say: “After copper has been refined, blackened, and later bleached; then (only) the tincture is solid.

Understand the six operations. Iosis is done by means of divine water; aflnning takes place in washing; blackening occurs when chrysolith is mixed (with burnt copper), before washing; attenuation, when it is released into chrysolith; bleaching, when it is dried after delaying with chrysolith; finally the yellowing can be applied when the yellowing is done.

Because often, the preparation being overabundant, the coatings were not fully absorbed and did not produce their specific effect. I will explain to you the comments of the oracle, I will explain to you what is there and all that the authors have said about it, and I will comment on it. Know, Osiris, that the oracle begins with yellowing, leaving aside the whitening. But he did not neglect the yellowing. Why not? He must be asked thoughtfully what he meant, and it is according to the dispositions of his mind that the oracle is interpreted. Orpheus proposed to carry out the laundering. sections.h: IV. VI. THE SPECIES IS COMPOSED AND NOT SIMPLE AND WHAT IS THE TREATMENT H)
p: Is it a simple thing or a thing composed, as to its nature, in art called in the masters the natural art? By nature, the golden soldering is a simple thing, a simple kind, according to the divine Hesiod and according to Aratus; it is this which is designated as a golden head, according to the divine prophet Daniel; as a golden choir, according to Hermes Trismegistus; but this is not what is meant by the sought unity. Art in reality must have neither a simple object nor an object composed of parts; for if the parts contained one and the same treatment, and did not differ in any way from each other, they would not be the parts of a complete whole. In fact, every natural or artificial part brings to the complete work something special; without it, the whole would be incomplete, as it is easy to see in the parts of the body, called places in Galen. This is how he can be heard to say, “Places are called parts of the body.” If any of these special parts fail, the composition will be found incomplete; either it has undergone only; the delay.

Taking female magnesia, grinds with care; put in dish

Good workmanship of the creator; success of the work and long life!

sections.h: PART V TECHNICAL TREATISES YI.- ON THE MOST PRECIOUS AND MOST PRECIOUS GOLDSMITHS
p: X This treatise is a workbook of practical craftsman, analogous to the Papyrus of Leide

(Introd. , p. 3. 19), to the technical recipes of the Pseudo-Democritus (p. 46), to the procedures of Jamblicus (p. 274), and to those of the Chemistry of Moses (see footnote at the bottom of page 288). According to the language, this text belongs to the popular Greek of the Middle Ages.
Manuscript A, which contains it, is a copy written in 1478; but the
) (; is roughly the same as that of two analogous articles, contained in Ms. M, written in the 12th century, one concerning hollow and embossed castings

; the other, lead and gold in sheets; these pieces will be given in the following part. These are indications to set the date of our treaty, or more precisely a limit of the date of the texts relating to this type of practice. Indeed, the original date of writing is certainly not the same for the various articles that the treaty contains: some being older and sometimes dating back to Egyptian Greco antiquity; while the others reproduce later recipes and perhaps contemporary additions of the last copyist. In any case, this treaty continues the old tradition of alchemical goldsmithing, which dates back to the ancient Egyptians. Tasem's name sometimes appears as

; distinct from that of money, and with the sense that he possessed h the origin IiiiroJ. , p. 3. 62); although there is often confusion, this word having ended up denoting silver as a variable of goldsmiths. Similarly, the word y sometimes denotes an alloy similar to silver and comparable to asem (v. 26); but it applies in other passages to mercury itself, as in neo-Greek: this is again a word whose meaning has changed in the course of the ages. The book ends with the reproduction of various texts by Zosirae: this shows the connectedness

traditional of the old Greek alchemy with the technical processes of the goldsmiths of the Middle Ages. All this, I repeat, is in accordance with the facts and ideas X developed in my Introduction, on the occasion of the recipes of the Papyrus of Leide.

1. To refine the gold. Take sea salt, put with solid lees; close the vase (pot?) at the top, and place it in the fireplace, until incandescent. Add, for a pound of this metal, 2 parts of sieved salt, and a third of crushed and sieved brick. Put in two pots, alternately, a layer of salt, and a layer of gold, thinned with the hammer as much as possible. Endure all around with the read of art. Then put it in the oven, so that the flame licks it. Now the furnace is arranged as follows. Taking a pot, pierce it from the center to the sides, from cross-shaped holes; add two fittings to it. Place the pots that contain the gold, in the middle of the cross, and in the lower layer of the pot makes a hole, so that the slag can escape. Then fill the furnace with coal and try to melt the gold. If the gold (is not) collected in the center, repeat the next day: soften the crushed brick with salt and repeat the operation, until you see the molten metal (i). 2. To refine the money. Prepare a crucible with ash and sieved brick; put a pound of asem into a crucible; cut into pieces

Other (recipe). Make the fine pearl macerate in a bird or in a pugnoneau, and let it be held there (until) the hour of the Pater noster; then press, in order to bring it out. 39. On the metal wires of goldsmiths. Taking pure money. soften it with the sevenfold of its weight of lead, (until) it becomes soft as gold. Then clean it and run it in a bar; bring it to a double length by threshing. Then make threads, leaves, branches, stars, roses, twisted and intertwined networks, animals, birds, and whatever else you want. Arranges a thin iron blade of uniform thickness. Take some gum, put it in a vase with water, and let it soak for one night; the morning pours out the water: to use it, put it in the fire, and brings in consistency of glue. Then take a hair clip, grab the threads or leaves one by one and place them in the glue. Then take them back, put them on the iron blade, and do whatever you want. sections.h: TECHNICAL TREATIES V. III. ON THE QUENCHING OF IRON
p: The tempering of iron, for almost everyone, is useful to know; it is multiple, as far as practice is concerned.

Take the goat horn; burn and grind it (ash so as to unite it with twice the salt, not by weight, but by volume. Add with the water you know (i), and knead to form a liquid paste. With this it is easy for you to get a sword of such quality as you want. You clean the edge of it; you put it on coals, and you make it blush at the desired point. After that, by throwing it into the water you know, you will have a sword made sharp by the quenching (which it has received). This tempering is, as Fa says, common and almost universally known. The projection in Skin must not be of any kind, but adjusted according to the shape and destination of the sword.

For instruments intended to cut stone and generally for all those who do not have a very sharp edge, it is enough to simply immerse them in water after heating. But tools that are otherwise, such as cutlasses and swords, should not be worked in any way: they are cooled with a wet cloth, or with a piece of damp wool, such as those used against the rain. We operate in the direction of the wire, covering the edge that must be soaked. That's the temper.
2. Second dip.

p: Taking soft iron, 4 pounds, cut it into small pieces; then taking from the bark of palm fruits (2), named elileg in the Arabs, i5 parts by weight, and 4 parts by weight of belileg (3), similarly cleaned inside, that is to say the bark alone; as well as 4 parts of ambileg-, similarly cleaned, and magnesia of glassmakers (4) mentioned above. Grind everything together, not too small, and mix with the 4 pounds of iron. Then put it in a crucible and equalize the place of the crucible before heating; for if you do not take this care, so that it (the crucible) is not moved, you will find difficulties in the operation of melting. Then put the coals and push the fire until the iron is melted, and the species (supposed) are united with it. The four pounds of iron require 100 pounds of coal. Observe that if iron is not very soft, it does not need magnesia, but only all other species; for magnesia makes it dry to the highest degree and it becomes brittle. But if it is sweet, it is necessary only to it, as it has been said above; for it accomplishes all. This is the first and royal operation, the one which is studied today, and by means of which wonderful swords are made. It was discovered by the Indians and exposed by the Persians, and it was from these that it came to us.

What species produce the coloration of (precious) stones and
BY WHAT treatment (i).

We know that the common agent in the works of this art is the comaris, and we propose to speak of the coloring of stones. Let us first see what species are liable to discolor the stones; how, united to the comaris, they color the glasses, or increase the tint of the natural (stones) what (are) the vases and the means of treatment.

As regards the manufacture of emeralds, according to the opinion of Ostanes, this universal compiler of the ancients, (the species employed are) the rust of copper, the biles of all sorts of animals and similar materials. For hyacinths (amethysts), the plant of the same name is used.
(jacinth) and the root of isatis, put into decoction with it.
For the carbuncle, it is the orcanette and the dragon blood.

For the carbuncle that shines at night, and which is called marine (purple) color, these are the biles of marine animals, fish or cetaceans; because of their property of shining at night, and especially their more or less glaucous color. This is what their entrails, scales and phosphorescent bones show. Mary says, “If you want to dye green, mix copper rust with turtle bile; if you want to get a more beautiful color, it’s with Indian turtle bile. Put the objects there, and (dyeing) will be quite top quality. If you do not have turtle bile, use blue marine lung (2), and you will make a more beautiful tincture. When fully developed, dyed objects emit a glow.
Thus Ostanes, for the emeralds, took the biles of the animals and the rust of the copper, without adding to it the marine color. For the hyacinth, he has

It should be noted that the biles of marine animals add phosphorescence to the specific coloration of each stone, when they are introduced in a suitable proportion into the dyeing (materials) specific to each color, or with certain other species. The treatises of the Greek-Egyptian Alchemists were collected by Zosimus first, in the middle of the century of our era, and then towards the "seen" century in the time of Heraclius, as it was exhibited in our Introduction (p. 200 to 2o3). They immediately became the object of multiplied commentaries, written by practitioners on the one hand, and by mystical philosophers on the other. With regard to the practical developments given to ancient doctrine, we shall recall that they were, from the time of Zosimus to the fourteenth century, and on some points to the end of the Middle Ages, recorded in treatises and in memoirs, of which our first five parts contain the remains. Among the most ancient mystical commentaries, of unquestionable philosophical significance, have been preserved in the works of Synesius and Olympus. Then came the Byzantine glossers, strangers to the experimental work, who dissected on the old treatises, with a scholastic subtlety mixed with exaltation. It is to this order of compositions that belong the books of Stephanus, the Christian Philosopher, and the Philosopher Anonymous. Stephanus is a well-known (i) character, both philosopher, physician, astrologer and alchemist, contemporary and advisor to the emperor Heraclius (around the year 620). His alchemical works, written in mystical and enthusiastic language, have little scientific interest; the Greek text of them was published by Ideler in his Physici et medici grœci minores (2 vols. in-8, Berlin I841-1842, p. 199-237) after a copy of Dietz, made on a Munich manuscript, and apparently co-ordinated on the old Venice manuscript, of which the Munich manuscript itself is a direct or indirect copy (2). This publication leaves much to be desired, the publisher having transi) Origins of Alchemy, . igq.

He writes the alchemical signs purely and simply, without understanding them, with more than one error, and having given no variant. However, it allows a sufficient knowledge of Stephanus' work; especially if it is completed by reading the Latin translation of this author, published in iby3 in Padua, by Pizimentius, in the work which bears the following title: Democrili de Arte magna. In these conditions, it did not seem essential to us to make a new edition of Stephanus, our publication being devoted essentially to original and unpublished works. It is otherwise the works of the Christian Philosopher and the Philosopher Anonymous, unpublished to this day. These are compilations, with comments, made according to the old authors. The initial extent of these compilations is not exactly known, since the copyists have successively attached pieces that were not originally part of it, as will be explained later. Some confusion even occurred between the two compilations. Finally, under the name of the Anonymous, it seems that several different authors have been grouped. One might doubt its rigor, if one were to attach himself to the quotation of the name Stephanus (i), reproduced in one of the chapters of the Christian: "On the detailed exposition of the work"; a chapter which we have published in the works of Zosimas (III, xvil, because of the indications contained therein and because it contains fragments taken from Democritus. But all these texts have been so interpolated by the copyists that one should not attach too absolute a meaning to such quotations, often added afterwards. In fact, I would be inclined to regard this quotation from Sergius as the only quite authentic one, and consequently to fix the date of the Christian at the time of this writer, that is to say, a little before Stephanus. It would also be postponed to a time that can hardly be lowered beyond the fifth or sixth century, by the opinions relating to the necessity of divine grace, opinions set forth in the piece VF, i, on the Constitution of gold (p. 385). As for the Philosopher Anonymous, he also quotes Stephanus, not in passing, but in a historical development relative to the alchemical authorities (VI, xiv), and I therefore think that he must be regarded as later. But it could be contemporary with the pseudonymous authors of the Lost Treatises, attributed to Heraclius and Justinian (2). The attribution of certain chapters to the Anonyme offers various confusions, which seem to indicate several writers. Let us now go into more detailed details about the compilation of the Christian. The most modern and perfect form under which we possessed this compilation is that which exists in the manuscript Lb (225 1 of Paris), copied towards the middle of the seventeenth century; in sight, it seems from a publication which did not take place. The copyist took as his basis the manuscript (2829 de Paris), a little older, which he first supplemented with marginal additions; he then subjected the texts to considerable reworkings, which most often are not improvements; finally he completed the compilation of the Christian, interspersing pieces that are not part of it with full certainty in the other manuscripts (except E. Let us now indicate the nature of the subjects treated and explain how we were led to dismember the compilation of the Christian, to carry a number of pieces in the previous parts. This dismemberment was indicated by our plan, in which I tried to reconstitute the texts with their oldest character. Now the compilation of the Christian was originally made under the general system followed by the Bvzantins, from the "vm" to the "x" century, during which time they drew from the ancient authors that they had in hand extracts and summaries, such as those of Photius and Constantine Porphyrogenete. This process has preserved for us a multitude of scraps of old texts; but it has contributed to make us lose the original works. A similar result was particularly regrettable with regard to scientific works, which their abbreviators misunderstood, neglecting the technical part to attach to the pieces.

Each of these (denominations) applied to yellow water, black water, white water; according to the different meanings adopted by the authors. But the diversity (of their explanations) produces a great embarrassment for readers. In fact, given the true (divine) unity of water, natural and general, as well as the unity of art, men find that it involves a multitude of treatments. By this they are led astray, being dominated by the respect and trust that the books inspire in them. But if they do not succeed in anything, they will necessarily be led to despise the books, at the same time as the art and the masters. However, the teachers, who had taught from their own point of view, were not the cause of the error of the young men, and the young men, on their side, who did not arrive at the result, did not act unjustly in attacking the elders.

sections.h: VI. IX. DIVISION OF THE MATERIAL
p: FROM THE DIVISION OF THE MATERIAL EX FOUR PARTS RESULT VARIOUS CLASSES OF MANUFACTURE, THEIR PARTS BEING SO SEPARATED, SO COMBINED WITH EACH OTHER. Ornithogonia (egg generation) is divided into four parts, I mean shell and hymen, white and yellow, and various classes, both general and special, have been rightly established. From the beginning, liquids from solids are treated separately, by the manufacture of water by means of stills. Then one deals with their union in the mortar; then again, beyond separation (of the materials) in the washings, until is dissipated, according to Democritus, the black coloration of the antimony. After that comes the distinction of the parts; then all the preparation is divided into two. But it is not a question of separation into its primitive components; for this is no longer possible after the combination formed by the emplastic iosis and the intimate and reciprocal mixture. Then the (first) half of the preparation is associated with various liquids, in the proportion of a cotyle for an ounce; which produces what is called gold liquor, silver liquor, or black efflorescence. While the other half, mixed with the materials that have been ground to the last degree of attenuation, realizes the desired product. Thus are manifested the branches of art which result from these divisions and the parts of matter, brought into harmony by a necessary law.

The famous philosopher of Abdera, Zosimas, John the Archpriest, Hermes Trismegistus, Democritus, Olympodorus and Stephanus, in the exhibition of the Chrysopaeus, revealed the mystery of the molybdochalchus(i); they agreed to take it as a starting point. In their memoirs based on experience, practice, and knowledge of matter, they prescribe the removal of all agents possessing caustic power, such as fire, sulfur, and all arsenic, because their mixture and strength are the source of all damage and accidents. But according to them it is necessary to use the mild agents, those which possess the liquefying power, for the mixing of the elements and the alloying of the lead. They also call this alloy union of substances: first when it is made by means of fusion, and also (when one operates) by roasting and washing. They designate (the molybdochalque) under the name of magnesia, because they mix, knead and quench, in order to bring the alloy to the state of a single substance, by the identification of the component substances. Now the mixture of the Whole, the (fabrication of) matter, is accomplished entirely by wet and by liquids; just as clay is kneaded with washed matter, such as cloths and bleached silks.

This is why Olympidore writes that the mystery of the Chrysopia lies in liquids. It is through the flow of water, currents, washings, maceration and treatment that the mysterious operation is carried out.

By these agents they are first liquefied, cooked, subjected to flow, by virtue of the resulting maceration and the operation of transmutation, and they thus change bodies. For they naturally pass into the incorporeal state, and they arrive in an extraordinary way at the state of cooked gold. Olympidore says (3): the molybdochalque or summer stone then determines the simultaneous flow of these products by fire. One of the effects is due to lead and the other to fire. It is not on one of the isolated materials that the simultaneous flow depends; but the matter must be made to flow by the association of the three products. They are first mixed in equal parts and to make them flow, one should not add one of the products to the other two, but mix at the same time the three in the same alloy. The word simultaneous flow shows that the whole must flow at a single stroke.
